name: Kubernetes
author: Smart Terminal
summary: Your clusters, and a terminal and a Claude session already pointed at what you are looking at.
description: Every cluster in your kubeconfig, browsable: nodes, workloads, config, network, storage and access, plus whatever custom resources the operators in that cluster installed — the navigation is built from what the cluster says it has, so nothing on it is a dead link. A table per kind with the columns that kind actually needs, a live status on every row, and a detail pane with the object's YAML, its events and its log. The log can be followed; a port of a pod, a service or a workload can be forwarded — kept by the app so it survives the panel being rebuilt, started again on the same local port when its connection drops, and opened in the browser with a click; and a workload can be scaled, rolled or deleted — the three that take something away stop and ask you first, naming the namespace and the cluster, because the same click is nothing in a scratch namespace and an outage in production. It never runs `use-context`: every call carries its own, so looking at a cluster here cannot change what your own shell does anywhere else. Two buttons make it more than a viewer. Shell opens a real terminal tab — a real pty in the app, not a toy inside a panel — running kubectl exec into the container you were looking at. And Ask Claude opens a session that has already been handed the description, the warning events and the log of the thing that is broken, including the log of the container that died. The YAML of any object can be edited and applied — always validated by the server first, and the question that stops you says whether Helm installed the thing you are about to change by hand. Helm itself is here too when the cluster has releases: every release with its revisions, the values it was installed with, what it actually put in the cluster, and a rollback on every revision that is not the current one. And the Map draws the same cluster as what is joined to what, three ways over one reading of it: Topology follows a request from ingress to service to workload to pods and on to the claim, the volume and the storage class behind it; Physical puts every pod inside the node it is actually running on, with remote volumes in a lane of their own rather than inside a machine they would outlive; Dependencies takes one workload and fans out everything it stands on, marks what every replica shares, and says what would go with a node, a zone or a storage class. What the API stated is drawn solid and what was worked out — that this StatefulSet is MongoDB, that this Deployment uses that service — is drawn dashed and says how. It never asks for a database password. From the same map a node pool can be cordoned, uncordoned or drained a node at a time, each behind a question that says how many nodes it is about. And what changes the machines themselves — a new node group, a pool moved onto another machine type, one resized or removed — is described in a form and handed to Claude with what the cluster says stands on those machines; the change is made where the node groups are defined, Terraform by default, a step at a time and only on your yes.
